title: Worse Overall, in 3D
eyebrow: CETI · the 75-second case · Simpson's paradox · WEBGL
lede: A new sales process converts worse overall, so it gets killed. Berkeley, 1973 is a city of 4,526 boxes: count the applicants in two columns, then fly the camera round to six department slabs.

commit.title: YOUR GUESS
commit.prompt: Women got in less often overall. In how many of the 6 departments did they do worse?

captions: Our new sales process converts worse overall.
So we killed it. Case closed?
Berkeley, 1973: women got in less often overall.
In how many of 6 departments did women do worse?
Fewer women got in. The headline writes itself.
Overall: 45 % of men admitted, 30 % of women.
Now split the same boxes by department.
Same boxes, same rules. Compare each department.
Women did worse in 2 of 6, by 3 and 4 points.
51 % of men applied to A or B. 7 % of women.
Monday: did the new process get the same mix of leads?
Splitting explains this gap. It does not prove fairness.

brand.takeaway: Split by segment before you call it worse.

factory/FORMAT.md and docs/DECISIONS.md Q13: the 8-second commit hold and the film-mode default guess (5).
honest: Splitting explains this gap. It does not prove fairness. The film counts the six largest departments of one year; why women applied mostly to the crowded departments is a question the split cannot answer.
Campus-wide the gap was about 44 % of 8,442 men against 35 % of 4,321 women (Bickel et al. 1975); pooled over the six departments shown it is 45 % against 30 %.
A split can mislead too: split on what came before the decision (the department, the segment), not on something the decision caused (Pearl 2014). The sales hook is a situation, not data.
